subject: deep-learning
question: Does word2vec give 'bank' different vectors in the two sentences?

artifact.setup:
Pretrained word2vec vectors, one per vocabulary word.
Sentences: "She sat on the river bank." / "She paid the cheque at the bank."
artifact.claim_in_notebook: "The 'bank' vectors in the two sentences differ, capturing the two meanings."

ai_claim: Yes. word2vec learns from context, so 'bank' in a river context and 'bank' in a money context get different vectors.

ai_solution.text: word2vec is trained on word contexts.
The two sentences have different contexts.
So 'bank' gets a different vector in each.
The vectors capture the two meanings.

failure.explanation: word2vec uses context during training but produces one fixed vector per word type. At lookup time, 'bank' maps to the same vector in both sentences - a blend of its senses. Contextual models (e.g. BERT-style encoders) produce different vectors depending on the sentence.
failure.why_convincing: Training on contexts makes it sound as if the vectors depend on context.

canonical_solution: No: word2vec is static; 'bank' has one vector regardless of the sentence. Use a contextual encoder to separate senses.

valid_evidence.summary: wv['bank'] is the same array for both sentences; cosine similarity 1.0.
A contextual encoder gives the two 'bank' tokens a cosine similarity of about 0.5.

counterexamples: Looking up 'bank' returns the identical vector every time.

hints.text: Ask whether a lookup table can depend on the sentence.
Step 3 assumes vectors change with context at use time.
Static embeddings have one vector per word; contextual embeddings vary per occurrence.
Compare wv['bank'] in both cases.
Step 3 is wrong: word2vec gives one vector per word. Use contextual embeddings.

repair: Use a contextual encoder (e.g. a sentence-transformer or BERT) when word sense matters.
debrief: Know whether your embeddings are per word type or per occurrence. It decides whether ambiguity can be resolved at all.

subject: deep-learning
subtopic: Fine-tuning with a large learning rate
question: Is lr = 0.1 on all layers a good way to fine-tune the pretrained model on 2,000 images?

artifact.code:
model = timm.create_model("resnet50", pretrained=True, num_classes=5)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)        # same as training from scratch
# Dataset: 2,000 labelled flower photos; all layers are trainable.

ai_claim: Yes. 0.1 is a standard learning rate for training ResNets, and training all layers lets the model adapt fully to flowers.

ai_solution.text: ResNets are commonly trained with lr = 0.1.
So the model adapts fully to the new task.
This is a good fine-tuning setup.

failure.misconception: Using a from-scratch learning rate for fine-tuning
failure.explanation: lr = 0.1 is chosen for random initialisation. Applied to pretrained weights, the large early updates (driven by the randomly initialised new head's gradients) overwrite the useful features - catastrophic forgetting - and with only 2,000 images the model then overfits. Use a much smaller learning rate (e.g. 1e-3 to 1e-4), lower rates for early layers, or freeze the backbone at first.
failure.why_convincing: It is a widely quoted, correct learning rate - for a different situation.

canonical_solution: No: a from-scratch learning rate destroys pretrained features. Use a small learning rate or freeze the backbone first.

valid_evidence.summary: Validation accuracy after 5 epochs: 61% with lr 0.1, 93% with lr 1e-3.
The first updates with a random head produce large gradients through the backbone, altering pretrained filters.

counterexamples: Fine-tuned with lr 0.1, the model does worse than a frozen backbone with a new head.

hints.text: Ask what the learning rate was originally chosen for.
Step 1 carries over a from-scratch setting.
Fine-tuning uses small learning rates to preserve pretrained features.
Compare lr 0.1 with 1e-3.
Step 1 is wrong: lr 0.1 overwrites pretrained features. Use a small learning rate.

repair: Freeze the backbone and train the head first, then unfreeze with lr around 1e-4 (discriminative learning rates).
debrief: Transfer learning works by keeping what the pretrained model knows. Learning rate is the main dial controlling how much is kept.

subject: deep-learning
subtopic: Feature extraction on a small dataset
question: Is the AI right that freezing the backbone and training only a linear head is a sensible approach with 500 images?

artifact.code:
backbone = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
backbone.fc = nn.Identity()
for p in backbone.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False
backbone.eval()
head = nn.Linear(512, 3)       # trained on 500 labelled photos of 3 kinds of leaves

ai_claim: Yes. With only 500 images, fine-tuning 11 million parameters would overfit. Using the frozen backbone's 512-dimensional features and training a 1,539-parameter head uses the pretrained knowledge with little risk of overfitting.

ai_solution.text: ResNet18 has about 11 million parameters; 500 images are too few to adapt them safely.
The frozen backbone provides general visual features learned from ImageNet.
The linear head has 512 x 3 + 3 = 1,539 parameters.
Training only the head suits the small dataset.

canonical_solution: Correct. For small datasets similar to natural images, feature extraction with a frozen backbone is the standard first approach (with eval mode so batch norm uses its pretrained statistics).

hints.text: Compare the number of images with the number of trainable parameters.
Step 3 counts the head's parameters.
With little data, train few parameters on top of pretrained features.
Count the head's parameters.
This solution is correct. A frozen backbone with a linear head suits 500 images. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: How much of a pretrained model to fine-tune depends on how much data you have and how similar it is to the pretraining data.

subject: deep-learning
question: Will ImageNet pretraining give a clear improvement over training from scratch?

artifact.plan: Fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 to detect pneumonia from chest X-rays.
artifact.unknown: How many labelled X-rays are available, and whether a model pretrained on medical images is an option, are not stated.

ai_claim: Yes. Pretraining always helps, because the model already knows how to see, so ImageNet pretraining will clearly beat training from scratch.

ai_solution.text: ImageNet models learn general visual features.
Pretraining will clearly beat training from scratch.

missing_information: The amount of labelled data and the domain gap. With a few thousand X-rays, ImageNet features (edges, textures) usually help substantially. With hundreds of thousands of labelled X-rays, training from scratch can match ImageNet initialisation, and grayscale medical images differ markedly from natural photos. Neither the dataset size nor alternative (medical) pretraining is given.
resolving_scenarios: 3,000 labelled X-rays: ImageNet initialisation converges faster and reaches clearly higher AUC than training from scratch.
300,000 labelled X-rays: from-scratch training reaches similar AUC, and the benefit of ImageNet pretraining is mainly faster convergence.
canonical_solution: It depends on data size and domain similarity, which are not given. Step 4 turns a common tendency into a guarantee.

valid_evidence.summary: With very large medical datasets, studies have found ImageNet pretraining gives little accuracy gain over random initialisation.

counterexamples: With abundant labelled X-rays, the gap can vanish.

hints.text: Ask how much labelled data is available.
Step 4 assumes pretraining always helps clearly.
Transfer benefit shrinks with more target data and a larger domain gap.
Compare 3,000 and 300,000 labelled images.
Step 4 is overconfident. With little data it helps; with much data it may not. It cannot be decided.

repair: Compare ImageNet initialisation, medical pretraining and training from scratch on a validation split.
debrief: Transfer learning is a strong default, not a law. Its benefit depends on data size and domain similarity.
